source_first_audit.profile_reason: integrate carries eight article senses across general combining, social membership, desegregation, the participial adjective and calculus, so the bounded inventory needs the extended source and fact allowance.
open_questions: The prescriptive negative claims in the usage notes (integrate A to B, integrate to, integrate in for the intransitive personal sense, and integrate by x for the calculus sense, and an integrated student for the adjective sense) rest on the absence of these patterns from the bounded source set. No dedicated counterexample search was run against a corpus within this budget.

No fact in this source set states a frequency band for any sense. Every numeric frequency score in the article is editorial calibration on the ten-point scale that entry_spec_v5 defines, not a corpus measurement. U-013 binds the frequency and register targets on that basis.

The register lines of senses 1 and 5 state that put together and combine, and fit in, are commoner than integrate in conversation. No fact in this source set compares the conversational frequency of two words, so these comparisons are the article's own judgment rather than source claims.

The register lines of the five general senses name business, technical, software, administrative, educational and personnel writing as the places integrate is common. No fact in this set carries a register or domain label for those senses, so those domain statements are the article's own judgment. The specialist labels on the desegregation and calculus senses and the regional labels are fact-backed.

The thesaurus facts F-015 and F-016 attest only the core synonym and antonym members. The article's other relation entries, among them interoperate, dovetail, standalone, all-white, keep to oneself, antidifferentiate and evaluate the integral, have no attesting fact in this set and are the article's own contrastive selection.

The transcriptions given for integrated and for the American form of integration are derived from the verb's transcription plus the regular -ed ending and the verb's second-syllable vowel, not quoted from a source. F-037 attests only that integrated has four syllables, and F-036 records only the British transcription of integration.

The etymology line glosses the cognate integral as both the calculus noun and the adjective meaning indispensable. F-046 attests the noun only; no fact in this set attests the adjectival sense. The same line glosses integrity with two readings; F-034 gives Latin integritatem as soundness, wholeness and completeness, which supports the completeness reading but not the modern moral one.

coverage_axes.notes: Four independent general dictionaries cover the combining, social, desegregation and calculus senses and the adjective.
Transitive, intransitive, reflexive, passive, attributive and calculus frames each have an independent source, and the inflected forms are listed.

integration, integrated, integrating, integrator, integrative, integrity, disintegrate, differentiate and the noun integral are each attested separately. The adjectival sense of integral that the etymology line also glosses is not attested here, as the open questions record.
The desegregation use, the calculus use and the electronics compound integrated circuit are each checked against a dictionary or a domain reference.

Adverb collocations, the American centre of gravity, the Northern Irish reading and the attested relation sets are sourced. Region is covered, and domain is covered for the senses the sources label as specialist. No fact states a frequency band, compares two words' conversational frequency, or labels the domain of the five general senses, so those three are editorial judgment, as the open questions record.

Two pronunciation references and one etymology reference cover the verb transcriptions, the syllable counts, the stress shift and the Latin origin. The transcriptions for integrated and the American form of integration are derived rather than sourced, as the open questions record.

sources.title: Cambridge Dictionary: integrate, and the pronunciation entries for integrate, integrated and integration

facts.statement: integrate combines two or more things so that they work as one more effective whole
facts.source_detail: Cambridge gives the transitive combining sense with the sales and marketing department example.

facts.statement: integrate helps a person become part of a group, and is also used of the person becoming part of that group
facts.source_detail: Cambridge lists both the causative use for helping someone join a group and the plain use for becoming part of one.

facts.statement: integrate is used both with a direct object and without one, and takes into and with
facts.source_detail: Cambridge marks transitive and intransitive uses and shows integrate into and integrate with.

facts.statement: integrate ends the separation of people by race, sex or national origin in an organization or in society
facts.source_detail: Cambridge gives the desegregation sense with the armed forces example and names race, sex and national origin.

facts.statement: integrate oneself takes a reflexive object in integrate oneself into a group, where the joining party is the subject
facts.source_detail: Cambridge's induction-programme example shows new staff members integrating themselves into the team.

facts.statement: integrate occurs without an object in integrate with one's colleagues and integrate socially
facts.source_detail: Cambridge shows Dave finding it hard to integrate with his colleagues and work that seems to have integrated socially.

facts.statement: integration is transcribed /ˌɪntɪˈɡreɪʃən/ with the primary stress on the third syllable, unlike the verb
facts.source_detail: Cambridge transcribes integration with primary stress on the GRAY syllable, the third of four.

facts.statement: integrated has four syllables, one more than the three-syllable integrate, the extra syllable being the -ed ending
facts.source_detail: Cambridge's integrated pronunciation entry has four syllables against the three of its integrate entry.

sources.title: Merriam-Webster: integrate, integrative, integrator, and the integrate thesaurus entry

facts.statement: integrate forms, coordinates or blends separate things into a functioning or unified whole
facts.source_detail: Merriam-Webster's first transitive sense is to form, coordinate, or blend into a functioning or unified whole; unite.

facts.statement: integrate incorporates something into a larger unit, or unites it with something else
facts.source_detail: Merriam-Webster's second transitive sense is to incorporate into a larger unit and to unite with something else.

facts.statement: integrate desegregates an institution and brings people into equal membership in society or an organization
facts.source_detail: Merriam-Webster's third transitive sense is to desegregate, with the school-districts example, and to end the segregation of and bring into equal membership.

facts.statement: integrate finds the integral of a function or equation
facts.source_detail: Merriam-Webster's fourth transitive sense is to find the integral of something such as a function or equation.

facts.statement: integrate has an intransitive use glossed as to become integrated
facts.source_detail: Merriam-Webster lists an intransitive entry for integrate meaning to become integrated.

facts.statement: integrative is an adjective meaning serving to integrate, favoring integration or directed toward integration
facts.source_detail: Merriam-Webster defines integrative as serving to integrate or favoring integration.

facts.statement: integrator is a noun for one that integrates, especially a device or computer unit that adds variable quantities in a manner comparable to mathematical integration
facts.source_detail: Merriam-Webster defines integrator as one that integrates, especially such a device or computer unit.

facts.statement: integrated and integrating are the inflected forms Merriam-Webster lists for the verb
facts.source_detail: Merriam-Webster's integrate entry lists the inflected forms integrated and integrating.

facts.statement: vertically integrated describes unified control of all stages of industrial production from raw materials to distribution
facts.source_detail: Merriam-Webster glosses vertically integrated as marked by unified control of all aspects of industrial production from raw materials through distribution.

facts.statement: integrate has join, unite, combine, blend, incorporate, merge, assimilate, amalgamate, coalesce, harmonize and meld listed as synonyms
facts.source_detail: The Merriam-Webster thesaurus entry for integrate lists these words among its synonyms.

facts.statement: integrate has separate, divide, part, segregate, split, decouple, detach, disperse and disband listed as antonyms
facts.source_detail: The Merriam-Webster thesaurus entry for integrate lists these words among its antonyms.

sources.title: Longman Dictionary of Contemporary English: integrate, integrated

facts.statement: integrate takes into for the receiving whole, as in integrating new ideas into the traditional course structure
facts.source_detail: Longman's integrate into example is the department successfully integrating new ideas into the traditional course structure.

facts.statement: integrate takes with for the matching counterpart, as in integrating one rail network with another
facts.source_detail: Longman's integrate with examples are the Italian railway network with other European networks and a computer program with existing programs.

facts.statement: integrate is commonly modified by completely, fully, seamlessly, thoroughly, properly and successfully
facts.source_detail: Longman's corpus notes list these adverbs as the usual modifiers of integrate.

facts.statement: integrated appears in the passive with in, as in disabled students are integrated in regular classrooms
facts.source_detail: Longman's corpus examples include disabled students being integrated in regular classrooms and bus and subway services being fully integrated.

facts.statement: integrated is an adjective for a system or institution that combines many different groups, ideas or parts so that they work well
facts.source_detail: Longman defines the adjective integrated with the integrated transport system example.

facts.statement: integrate is used of people becoming fully integrated into a local community
facts.source_detail: Longman's example is that they soon became fully integrated into the local community.

facts.statement: integrated describes something in which many different parts are closely connected and work successfully together
facts.source_detail: Oxford's first adjective sense is in which many different parts are closely connected and work successfully together.

facts.statement: integrated describes an institution intended for use by all races or religious groups, including people from different races, sexes or religions who were previously separated
facts.source_detail: Oxford's second adjective sense covers integrated institutions intended for all races or religious groups, naming race, sex and religion rather than race alone.

facts.statement: integrate is given for Standard Southern British as /ˈɪn.tɪ.ɡɹeɪt/ with an /ˈɪn.tə.ɡɹeɪt/ variant
facts.source_detail: Wiktionary lists the British pronunciation with the second-syllable vowel written /ɪ/ and a /ə/ variant.

facts.statement: integrate is given for General American as /ˈɪn.təˌɡɹeɪt/ with secondary stress on the third syllable
facts.source_detail: Wiktionary lists the General American pronunciation with a secondary stress mark before the third syllable.

facts.statement: integrate carries primary stress on the first syllable in both the British and the American transcription
facts.source_detail: Both Wiktionary transcriptions place the primary stress mark before the first syllable.

facts.statement: integrate is attested as an adjective from the 1450s, earlier than the verb, which is seventeenth century
facts.source_detail: Wiktionary records the adjective from the 1450s and the verb from the seventeenth century.

facts.statement: integrate comes from Latin integratus, past participle of integrare to make whole, from integer whole
facts.source_detail: Etymonline derives integrate from Latin integratus, the past participle of integrare, from integer.

facts.statement: integer is literally untouched, from in- not plus the root of tangere to touch
facts.source_detail: Etymonline glosses Latin integer as whole, complete, literally untouched, from in- not and the root of tangere.

facts.statement: integrate is recorded as a verb from the 1630s meaning to render something whole by bringing together its parts
facts.source_detail: Etymonline dates the verb to the 1630s with the sense to render (something) whole, bring together the parts of.

facts.statement: integration is recorded from the 1610s as the act of bringing together the parts of a whole
facts.source_detail: Etymonline dates integration to the 1610s from Late Latin integrationem.

facts.statement: integrity is from about 1400, from Latin integritatem soundness, wholeness, completeness
facts.source_detail: Etymonline dates integrity to around 1400 from Old French integrite and Latin integritatem.

facts.statement: disintegrate is dated 1796, formed from dis- do the opposite of plus integrate, first used in geology for separating into component parts and destroying cohesion, with the intransitive break-apart sense by 1851
facts.source_detail: Etymonline dates disintegrate to 1796 from dis- plus integrate and records the intransitive sense from 1851.

facts.statement: integrate is used intransitively of one thing integrating with another, the two becoming closely linked or forming part of one whole idea or system
facts.source_detail: Collins states that if you integrate one thing with another, or one thing integrates with another, the two things become closely linked or form part of a whole idea or system.

facts.statement: integrate takes a non-human subject in the intransitive frame, as when one part of a building is to integrate with another
facts.source_detail: Collins illustrates the intransitive use with a non-human subject: Ann wanted the conservatory to integrate with the kitchen.

sources.title: Wikipedia: School integration in the United States; Integrated education in Northern Ireland; Integral

facts.statement: integrate names the American process of ending race-based segregation in public and private schools
facts.source_detail: The School integration in the United States article describes it as the process of ending race-based segregation in American schools.

facts.statement: integrate is anchored in American usage to the civil-rights era opened by the 1954 Brown v. Board of Education ruling against school segregation
facts.source_detail: The School integration in the United States article treats the 1954 Brown v. Board of Education decision, which aimed to end school segregation, as the turning point of the process.

facts.statement: integrated names schools in Northern Ireland that teach Catholic and Protestant children together, a religious rather than a racial separation
facts.source_detail: The Integrated education in Northern Ireland article describes integrated schools as bringing together children from Catholic, Protestant and other backgrounds.

facts.statement: integrate is contrasted in American writing with desegregation, which removes the legal separation without producing a mixed body
facts.source_detail: Writing on American schools distinguishes legally desegregated schools that remain almost entirely single-race from integrated ones.

facts.statement: integrate is performed with respect to a named variable, written as an integral of f(x) with dx
facts.source_detail: The Integral article writes definite and indefinite integrals with respect to a variable of integration marked by dx.

facts.statement: integrate is performed over an interval from a lower limit to an upper limit for a definite integral
facts.source_detail: The Integral article defines the definite integral over an interval bounded by limits a and b.

facts.statement: integrate is done by parts as a named standard technique, and numerically when no closed form exists
facts.source_detail: The Integral article lists integration by parts among the standard techniques and numerical integration for cases without a closed form.

facts.statement: differentiate is the inverse operation of integration under the fundamental theorem of calculus
facts.source_detail: The Integral article states that integration is the inverse operation of differentiation.

facts.statement: integral is the noun for the object that integration produces, the quantity obtained by integrating a function
facts.source_detail: The Integral article defines the integral as the quantity produced by integration, assigning numbers to functions to describe area, volume and accumulation.

facts.statement: integrated circuit is a set of electronic circuits on one small flat piece of semiconductor material, normally silicon
facts.source_detail: The Integrated circuit article defines it as a set of electronic circuits on one small flat piece of semiconductor material.

facts.statement: integer is the mathematical term for a whole number, covering the natural numbers, their negatives and zero
facts.source_detail: The Integer article defines integers as the whole numbers: the natural numbers, their negatives and zero.

source_union.canonical_statement: integrate combines separate elements, functions or units so that the whole works as one
source_union.rationale: Three independent general dictionaries give the transitive combining sense, both prepositional frames and the adverb collocations.

source_union.canonical_statement: integrated is an established adjective for a whole whose many parts are closely connected and work together
source_union.rationale: Two independent learner dictionaries list the adjective separately from the verb, which supports a numbered participial-adjective sense, and the electronics reference fixes the integrated circuit compound the block glosses.

source_union.canonical_statement: integrate is used without an object of systems and services that come to work together
source_union.rationale: Collins states the intransitive frame directly and illustrates it with a non-human subject, which is what separates this sense from the intransitive personal sense; the Merriam-Webster intransitive entry and the Cambridge transitivity note carry the rest.

source_union.canonical_statement: integrate takes a person or group as object when an institution makes them a full member of a community, and takes a reflexive object when the joining party acts on itself
source_union.rationale: The causative use with a personal object, the reflexive frame and the passive with in are attested independently of the combining sense.

source_union.canonical_statement: integrate is used without an object of a person who becomes a full member of a group or community
source_union.rationale: The objectless personal use and the fully integrated into a community example support a separate intransitive sense.

source_union.canonical_statement: integrate ends a separation by race, sex or national origin in an institution and brings people into equal membership
source_union.rationale: Two general dictionaries give a scope wider than race alone, and the domain reference supports the American centre of gravity and the contrast with desegregate.

source_union.canonical_statement: integrated describes a school, district or neighbourhood that no longer separates people by race or by religion
source_union.rationale: The learner dictionary adjective sense names race, sex and religion, and the domain reference supplies both the American racial reading and the Northern Irish religious one.

source_union.canonical_statement: integrate finds the integral of a function with respect to a variable, over limits, by parts or numerically
source_union.rationale: The dictionary sense fixes the lexical meaning and the domain reference fixes the frames and the inverse relation to differentiation.

source_union.canonical_statement: integrate carries first-syllable primary stress with a British and American difference in the second-syllable vowel and the third-syllable secondary stress, while integrated adds a syllable and integration shifts the primary stress
source_union.rationale: Two independent pronunciation references cover the verb transcriptions, the four-syllable count of integrated and the British transcription and stress shift of integration. They do not give a transcription for integrated or an American transcription for integration; the article derives those from the verb, and the open questions record it.

source_union.canonical_statement: integrate descends from Latin integer whole and keeps a modern core of making separate things into one undivided whole
source_union.rationale: The etymology reference supports the origin, the two dates and the related words, the mathematical references fix the glosses given for integer and the noun integral, and the shared core is what the core-image branches use.

source_union.canonical_statement: the integrate family produces integration, integrated, integrating, integrator, integrative and disintegrate
source_union.rationale: Each derived or inflected form listed in the article has its own dictionary or etymology fact, including the 1796 formation of disintegrate.

source_union.canonical_statement: integrate has a thesaurus-attested core of near-synonyms and opposites, which the article extends with further contrasts of its own
source_union.rationale: F-015 and F-016 attest only the core members: combine, merge, incorporate, blend and assimilate among the synonyms, separate and segregate among the antonyms; F-044 attests differentiate as the inverse of integration. The article's remaining relation entries, among them interoperate, dovetail, standalone, all-white, keep to oneself, antidifferentiate and evaluate the integral, are contrasts the article selects to mark usage boundaries, and their definition, frequency and difference lines are the article's own analysis rather than claims taken from this source set. The open questions record that gap.

source_union.canonical_statement: the specialist and regional labels attached to the senses follow the cited entries, while the domain statements of the five general senses and the ten-point frequency scores are the article's own judgment
source_union.rationale: These facts fix the labelled parts of the register lines: the specialist scope of the desegregation and calculus senses, the adverb collocations, the institutional scope of the adjective, the American centre of gravity and the Northern Irish reading. Three things in these lines are the article's own judgment rather than source claims: the numeric scores, which are editorial calibration on the ten-point scale that entry_spec_v5 defines; the comparative statements that another word is commoner in conversation than integrate; and the domain statements attached to the five general senses, which name business, technical, software, administrative, educational and personnel writing without a labelling fact behind them.
